title: MIC vs. MBC

references.label: Biosafety in Microbiological and Biomedical Laboratories (BMBL)

summary: MIC (Minimum Inhibitory Concentration) is the lowest antimicrobial concentration that visibly inhibits growth. MBC (Minimum Bactericidal Concentration) is the lowest concentration that kills a defined proportion (commonly cited as ≥99.9%) of the original inoculum.
explanation: MIC is typically determined by broth microdilution or a similar method, reading for visible turbidity/no growth. MBC is determined by subculturing wells at or above the MIC onto antibiotic-free media and looking for the concentration at which the required kill proportion is achieved. MBC is always greater than or equal to MIC for a given organism-drug pair — an agent that merely inhibits growth (bacteriostatic) will have an MBC much higher than its MIC, or none determinable at tested concentrations, while a bactericidal agent's MBC is close to its MIC. Full determination methodology is a Tier 2 protocol topic; this entry defines the terms only.

comparison.left: MIC: lowest concentration that inhibits visible growth
comparison.right: MBC: lowest concentration that kills a defined proportion of the inoculum
MBC ≈ MIC suggests a bactericidal agent; MBC ≫ MIC suggests bacteriostatic

commonMisconceptions: Treating MIC as if it always tells you whether an agent kills the organism — it only tells you it stops visible growth.
